title: My Heart Has Sobered from Salma and Its Folly Has Ceased
intro: Zuhayr praises Hisn ibn Hudhayfa of Fazara. Tha'lab relates that Hisn sheltered a man wanted by al-Nu'man and refused to hand him over. The poem moves from grey hair and the memory of Salma to a hunt in which even bridling the horse takes several men, then brings us close enough to see Hisn’s face as he welcomes someone in need. Al-Shantamari’s recension ends with two verses about a man who starts a quarrel and then comes over to ask what happened. Abu Ubayd quotes the first of these under the name of Khawwat ibn Jubayr.

translation: My heart has sobered from Salma and its folly has ceased.
Youth’s horses and riding camels have been unsaddled.
1.sharh: Love has been an intoxication from which the heart wakes. Unsaddling every kind of mount makes the change visible in the camp, where a journey once possible no longer seems about to begin.

translation: I have given up what you know of, and every turning
has been closed to me save the straight course.
2.sharh: “What you know” leaves an old intimacy intact even as he renounces it. He imagines the change in his conduct as a road whose inviting turnings have all been closed.

translation: The girls said, “You are our uncle now.”
Youth was a companion from whom we parted.
3.sharh: “Uncle” is kindly enough, but it tells him he has crossed into another generation. Youth itself becomes one of the companions from whom a man has to take leave.

translation: Now all they recognise is my disposition,
and my black hair, with grey spreading through it.
4.sharh: Temperament is something the girls can still recognise. In his hair they can see the two ages together, black strands remembered and grey already overtaking them.

translation: Whose camp traces are these, like writing, their dwellings worn away?
Al-Rass has faded there, then al-Rusays and Aqil.
5.sharh: The marks of habitation are as legible, and as difficult to read, as lines on a page. The people are gone, but he can still give their landscape its names.

translation: Then Raqd and Sarat and the outskirts of Man'ij,
then east of Salma, its basin and its hollows.
6.sharh: The names take his eye from the margins of one district to water-holding hollows in the next. Here Salma names a mountain, an echo of the woman whose name opened the poem.

translation: Then the valley of al-Badi, al-Tawi and Thadiq,
then al-Qanan’s valley, its bend and its outlying places.
7.sharh: Each “then” carries him another stretch. Instead of one isolated ruin we have a succession of watercourses, bends and outlying ground that his listeners could follow.

translation: And many a tract of first rains, its gullies dark green,
its uplands answering the showers and steady downpours,
8.sharh: The channels have gone so densely green that they look dark. Where the camps had barely left a mark, rain now gets an answer from the higher ground in the form of growth.

translation: I rode down on a horse of taut sinews, swimming in stride,
firmly knit, smooth-cheeked and full where the heels touch.
9.sharh: The horseman sees the smooth cheek, but knows the horse’s barrel by the pressure of his own heels. “Swimming” gives the powerful frame an unexpectedly fluid motion.

translation: A well-made colt, we weaned him and his shape filled out.
He reached his prime, made strong by forelegs and withers.
10.sharh: He can remember the horse before its present strength was apparent. The forelegs and withers are his evidence that a colt raised by his own people has come good.

translation: Sound in the bones of his legs, his skin never pierced
by a farrier’s iron, his leg veins never cut.
11.sharh: His bill of health takes the form of a farrier’s examination. The poet knows which bones and veins would show the marks of an earlier ailment.

translation: When we ride out of a morning looking for game,
once we see it we have no need of stealth.
12.sharh: The horse gives its riders the luxury of an open chase. Once the animal is in sight, they can dispense with the usual care of creeping up on it.

translation: While we were looking for game our lad came up,
stealing along, hiding himself and crouching low.
13.sharh: The scout arrives doing precisely what the boastful hunters need not do. His effort to make himself small is the first sign that there is something nearby worth seeing.

translation: He said, “Game is grazing out in open country,
where growth fills the channels and the watercourses are dark green.
14.sharh: His report begins with the grazing ground. The broad word for the animals leaves their identity open until he brings the little herd into focus.

translation: Three like bows of sara wood, and a jack
with green lips from nibbling the grass beneath the old growth.
15.sharh: The three curved shapes are she-asses, accompanied by a wild jack. The scout has seen him closely enough to report the green stain of young grass on his lips.

translation: Hunters have taken his young from him one by one.
Only he and his mates are left.”
16.sharh: The missing foals acquire a history. Calling the remaining females his wives gives the hunted animal a household just as the men are deciding what to do about him.

translation: My companion said, “What do you think of what we see?
Shall we catch him unawares or challenge him openly?”
17.sharh: The boast about speed becomes a practical choice put to another man. The two verbs allow for a trick or an open match, almost as though the wild ass could accept a challenge.

translation: We spent the night stripped down at our horse’s head.
He struggled to get free of us and we struggled with him.
18.sharh: Before there can be a contest with the quarry there is one at the horse’s head. The same verb passes back and forth between the animal and the men trying to hold him.

translation: We struck him till the nape of his neck was still.
His heart and the muscles knotted in him were still racing.
19.sharh: The men have got one part of the horse to be still. Deeper down the heart and the bundles of muscle remain in furious motion.

translation: Our bridler can scarcely reach his nape.
Only the tips of his toes can reach the ground.
20.sharh: For the scale of the horse’s resistance he gives us the man at the bridle. His reach is stretched until almost nothing of his feet is left on the ground.

translation: With effort after effort we got our young rider up
onto that close-woven back, its joints lean and hard.
21.sharh: The repeated word for difficulty slows the mounting down. Once the boy is up, the horse beneath him feels like tight weaving over clean, spare joints.

translation: I told him, “Keep straight, watch the way he goes.”
What he is doing takes his mind off my advice.
22.sharh: The advice comes from a man with time to see the whole field. Atop the excited horse the boy is already too occupied to attend to every word.

translation: I told him, “Know that game has its unguarded instant.
If you do not waste it, you will kill him.”
23.sharh: After all the labour of getting ready, success turns on one instant. He wants the boy to recognise it before the hunted animal is alert again.

translation: Our lad followed the tracks of the herd
like a burst of rain lashing the hillocks with its downpour.
24.sharh: Rain first made the pasture that drew the animals there. Now a violent squall sweeping the hillocks supplies the measure of the rider’s rush.

translation: I looked towards him and in that one glance saw him
carrying his rider on through every change of fortune.
25.sharh: Horse and rider are almost one figure at this distance. Tha'lab’s commentary also preserves a second way to take the shifting pronouns, with the boy driving the horse as the chase demands.

translation: They fling gravel in his face, yet he closes in,
his hind legs swift, his forelegs sure of their aim.
26.sharh: The gravel striking his face measures how nearly he has caught them. The rear of his body supplies speed and the front supplies direction.

translation: He turned the wild jack back to us, cut off from his mates,
against his will, his leg and haunch veins bleeding.
27.sharh: Turning the jack away from his companions completes the boy’s manoeuvre. Blood at the thigh and hip tells what the wound has done without recounting the stroke.

translation: We came home with the horse outstripping the thoroughbreds at dusk,
his pasterns and weight-bearing legs dyed red.
28.sharh: The stain on the horse belongs to the game it helped to bring down. Even on the way home it leaves other good horses behind.

translation: Such a burst of speed, the place where a lance rests
never giving way to slowness, the hindquarters never failing it.
29.sharh: A lance could rest across the withers. The phrase marks the front of the horse so that we can feel how well the hindquarters keep pace with it.

translation: And a noble, lavish man, his hands a cloud
over those who come in need, his gifts missing no day.
30.sharh: A raincloud returns in the form of Hisn’s hands. What fed the pasture and pictured a rider’s speed now measures the reliability of a man’s giving.

translation: I went to him early and found
his reprovers seated beside him in the dawn light.
31.sharh: He comes upon a domestic council already in progress. “Sirim” can place it at the end of night or the start of morning, and was also understood as a stretch of sand.

translation: Now they offer their lives for him, now they blame him.
He defeats them. They cannot see how to get round him.
32.sharh: The affectionate formula “May I be your ransom” alternates with straight reproach. Neither approach finds a way past his determination to keep giving.

translation: They desisted before a generous man much resorted to,
set on doing what he means to do.
33.sharh: Petitioners repeatedly make inroads on his resources. The women have tried their arguments on a man who counts giving those resources away among his settled intentions.

translation: A man to trust, whose wealth wine does not waste,
though his giving may well consume it.
34.sharh: A household could lose its fortune either way. The distinction is whether the expenditure buys the owner pleasure or meets someone else’s need.

translation: When you come to him you see his face light up,
as though you were giving him the very thing you ask.
35.sharh: The petitioner sees pleasure before receiving a gift. For an instant the expression on Hisn’s face exchanges the roles of giver and receiver.

translation: You have reached out to a man of distant kin
with money, before he even knew you meant to help.
36.sharh: The branch of the family is distant and the recipient has made no approach. Hisn can see the connection, and the need, before the other man realises that help is coming.

translation: A kindness you brought to completion and acknowledged,
an opponent whose false case nearly defeated the truth,
37.sharh: Acknowledging kindness is one form of sound judgement. The next requires him to answer a persuasive opponent, and for a line we are left waiting to hear how he answers.

translation: you turned aside with a fair, well-aimed word,
when the points of the dispute baffled other speakers.
38.sharh: His reply finds the joint at which the dispute can be resolved. The image allows us to feel what it means to cut an argument precisely where other speakers have fumbled.

translation: And a man wild in speech who thinks himself right,
saying whatever happens to enter his head,
39.sharh: This speaker cannot tell a passing thought from a good argument. Hisn will have to exercise a different kind of judgement with a man who says everything he thinks.

translation: you mustered patience for him and honoured someone else.
You turned away, though his vulnerable places lay bare.
40.sharh: Hisn has the means to hurt the man and the self-command to leave them unused. Giving his attention to someone else is itself his public answer.

translation: Hudhayfa raises him, and Badr, both of them,
to a height above anyone who would rival him.
41.sharh: His father and grandfather now come into view. Their elevation follows a long account of Hisn’s own conduct, so inherited standing has concrete examples behind it.

translation: Who equals Hisn in war, who equals him
at resisting a wrong or pursuing what he undertakes?
42.sharh: The question finally names the man whose face and conduct we already know. His refusal of injury is immediately put to a particularly demanding test.

translation: He refused submission while al-Nu'man ground his fang at him.
He went out into the open, his swords his strongholds.
43.sharh: A king’s anger is visible in the grinding tooth. Out on open ground, Hisn possesses the protection a city might give, condensed into the swords around him.

translation: Unassailable when the two allies camp around him
with a clamorous host, its uproar and its neighing horses.
44.sharh: The two allies are Asad and Ghatafan. Men and horses make different sounds that reach us together, giving Hisn’s security an audible scale.

translation: For him the country shakes as far as the sands of Alij.
A lowlander’s upheavals fall away.
45.sharh: The army’s weight is felt to distant dunes, while people in the low country feel their troubles cease. Al-Asma'i takes the second shaking as calamities dispelled by the chief.

translation: And people of a tent, once on good terms,
fell to fighting over something sudden that I brought about.
46.sharh: The speaker admits that a sudden quarrel in a peaceful household was his doing. The two similar-sounding words play on an expectation of “now” and “later”, then reveal a culprit.

translation: I came up with the men hurrying over and asked after them,
the way you ask about a thing you know nothing of.
47.sharh: He joins the people arriving to find out what happened and asks an innocent’s question. The listener has just been taken into his confidence and knows exactly how disingenuous it is.

1.1.4.meaning: Salma is the woman whose love opens the poem. Her name returns as the name of a mountain in verse 6.

1.1.5.head: أَقصَرَ
1.1.5.meaning: Desisted. What the heart has given up here is its youthful pursuit of pleasure.

1.2.1.head: عَرّى
1.2.1.meaning: Stripped the mounts of their tack, as at the end of a journey.

1.2.4.head: راحِلَة
1.2.4.meaning: A riding camel fit for a journey. The horses and camels together make up the mounts of youth.

2.2.3-4.head: قَصد السَّبيل
2.2.3-4.meaning: “The straight course of the road”, hence a steady, sober course in life.

2.2.5.head: مَعدِل
2.2.5.meaning: A turning off the main road, here one of the distractions once open to him.

3.1.2.head: عَذراء
3.1.2.meaning: Young women of marriageable age. Their form of address places him in an older generation.

3.2.3.head: خَليط
3.2.3.meaning: A close companion, or the people who share a camp until the time comes to move away.

3.2.4.head: زايَلَ
3.2.4.meaning: Parted company. He speaks of his youth as someone from the old camp.

4.1.5.head: خَليقَة
4.1.5.meaning: Disposition, the enduring trait by which the girls can still recognise him.

5.1.2.head: طَلَل
5.1.2.meaning: A surviving trace of an abandoned camp, especially one still visible above ground.

5.1.3.head: وَحي
5.1.3.meaning: Writing or an inscription. The scant marks of the camp resemble written strokes.

5.1.4.head: عَفا
5.1.4.meaning: Worn away until the traces are faint.

5.2.2.head: الرَّسّ
5.2.2.meaning: Al-Rass is a watering place of Banu Asad, named with al-Rusays.

5.2.4.head: الرُّسَيس
5.2.4.meaning: Al-Rusays is another watering place in the country of Banu Asad.

5.2.5.head: عاقِل
5.2.5.meaning: Aqil is a place on the poet’s itinerary through the deserted country.

6.1.1.head: رَقد
6.1.1.meaning: Raqd is a place in the sequence of camp sites. Tha'lab’s text names al-Qaff here.

6.1.2.head: صارات
6.1.2.meaning: Sarat is the name of a group of hills. A single one is a sara.

6.1.3-4.head: أَكناف مَنعِج
6.1.3-4.meaning: “The flanks of Man'ij”, the country around a place belonging to Banu Asad.

6.2.2.meaning: Salma is one of the two mountains of Tayyi'. The poet names its eastern side.

6.2.4.head: أَجاوِل
6.2.4.meaning: Margins or sides of the land. The commentators also record a place-name, Ajawil.

7.1.1-2.head: وادي البَدِيّ
7.1.1-2.meaning: Wadi al-Badi is a valley named on the route across the old camping grounds.

7.1.3.head: الطَّوِيّ
7.1.3.meaning: Al-Tawi is a place-name in this account of the country around the camps.

7.1.4.head: ثادِق
7.1.4.meaning: Thadiq is the next place after al-Tawi in this version of the itinerary.

7.2.1-2.head: وادي القَنان
7.2.1-2.meaning: Wadi al-Qanan takes its name from a mountain in the country of Banu Asad.

7.2.3.head: جِزع
7.2.3.meaning: A bend or side of a valley where its course changes.

7.2.4.head: أَفاكِل
7.2.4.meaning: Afakil are the outlying parts of the valley in the gloss on this reading.

8.1.3.head: وَسمِيّ
8.1.3.meaning: Wasmi is the first seasonal rain, so called for the mark of growing plants it leaves.

8.1.4.head: أَحوى
8.1.4.meaning: Dark green almost to black. The plural describes the densely grown channels.

8.1.5.head: تَلعَة
8.1.5.meaning: A rain channel descending from high ground into the valley.

8.2.2.head: رابِيَة
8.2.2.meaning: A rise of ground. Its answer to the rain is the growth it sends up.

8.2.3.meaning: Rainclouds or their first rain. Another gloss takes the word as high ground.

8.2.4.head: هاطِل
8.2.4.meaning: A shower whose heavy drops follow one another continuously.

9.1.2-3.head: مَمسود النَّواشِر
9.1.2-3.meaning: “Tightly twisted foreleg sinews”. The cords stand out on the horse like well-made rope.

9.1.4.head: سابِح
9.1.4.meaning: A horse whose extended forelegs in full stride suggest swimming.

9.2.1.head: مُمَرّ
9.2.1.meaning: Firmly knit, like a rope drawn tight in the twisting.

9.2.4-5.head: نَهد المَراكِل
9.2.4-5.meaning: “Full where the heels strike”, describing the flanks against the rider’s heels.

10.1.1.head: تَميم
10.1.1.meaning: Soundly formed. The word here describes the colt’s build.

10.1.2.head: فَلا
10.1.2.meaning: Weaned the foal. Another transmission has a verb meaning “we fed him”.

10.2.2.head: عَزَّ
10.2.2.meaning: Made strong. The forelegs and withers account for the horse’s strength.

10.2.4.head: كاهِل
10.2.4.meaning: The withers, the ridge where a horse’s neck and back meet above the shoulders.

11.1.2.head: شَظى
11.1.2.meaning: A small splint bone alongside a horse’s foreleg. Its soundness matters to the horse’s gait.

11.1.5.head: صِفاق
11.1.5.meaning: Skin or membrane, here on the belly where a farrier might have to pierce it.

11.2.1.head: مِنقَبَة
11.2.1.meaning: A piercing iron used by the farrier in treating an animal.

11.2.4.head: أَبجَل
11.2.4.meaning: A vein. The commentary locates these veins in the horse’s forelegs.

12.2.5.head: خاتَلَ
12.2.5.meaning: Stalked by stealth, trying to catch the game unawares.

13.1.2.head: بَغّى
13.1.2.meaning: Sought out, here ranging in search of game.

13.2.4.head: ضاءَلَ
13.2.4.meaning: Made himself small, crouching to avoid being seen.

14.1.2.head: شاة
14.1.2.meaning: Game animals seen at a distance. The following verse identifies the wild asses.

14.2.1-2.head: مُستَأسِد القُريان
14.2.1-2.meaning: “Luxuriant growth in the channels”. A qari carries runoff down to the meadows.

14.2.4.head: مَسيل
14.2.4.meaning: A watercourse, now filled with dark green growth.

15.1.3.head: السَّراء
15.1.3.meaning: Sara is a tree used for bow wood. Its curved bows recall the she-asses’ bodies.

15.1.4.head: مِسحَل
15.1.4.meaning: A wild jackass, named here by a word associated with its braying.

15.2.4.head: لَسّ
15.2.4.meaning: Nibbling with the front of the mouth.

15.2.5.head: غَمير
15.2.5.meaning: Fresh grass growing beneath last season’s dry cover.

15.2.6.head: جَحفَلَة
15.2.6.meaning: The lip of a hoofed animal. It bears the green stain of grazing.

16.1.2.meaning: Reduced little by little. The hunters have taken the jack’s young one by one.

16.2.5.head: حَليلَة
16.2.5.meaning: A wife. The wild jack’s female companions are given a human kinship term.

17.1.2.head: أَمير
17.1.2.meaning: A companion consulted about a decision. Tha'lab explains the word through the verb for taking counsel.

17.2.5.head: صاوَلَ
17.2.5.meaning: Closed with an opponent in open contest, the alternative to stalking the animal.

18.1.2.head: عُراة
18.1.2.meaning: Stripped for the work of handling the horse. Another gloss understands men on foot.

18.2.1.head: زاوَلَ
18.2.1.meaning: Struggled or wrestled. The animal is trying to free himself from his handlers.

19.1.4.head: قَذال
19.1.4.meaning: The nape or poll, close to the upper part of the bridle.

19.2.4.head: خَصيلَة
19.2.4.meaning: A bundle of muscle. The horse’s muscles keep quivering after its head is still.

20.1.1.head: مُلجِم
20.1.1.meaning: The person fitting the horse’s bridle.

20.2.5.head: أَنمُلَة
20.2.5.meaning: The tip of a digit, here the toes, the man’s only contact with the ground.

21.1.1-2.head: لَأياً بِلَأي
21.1.1-2.meaning: “Difficulty upon difficulty”, with painstaking effort and delay.

21.2.3.head: مَحبوك
21.2.3.meaning: Tightly woven, applied to the compact muscles along the horse’s back.

21.2.4-5.head: ظِماء المَفاصِل
21.2.4-5.meaning: “Thirsty joints”, a horseman’s image for lean, hard joints.

22.1.3.meaning: Keep straight and direct the horse towards its quarry.

22.2.5.head: وَصاة
22.2.5.meaning: A piece of counsel, the instruction given to the young rider.

23.1.2.meaning: Know or bear in mind, introducing a piece of hunters’ experience.

23.1.5.head: غِرَّة
23.1.5.meaning: An unguarded instant in which game can be taken.

24.2.1.head: شُؤبوب
24.2.1.meaning: A sudden, concentrated burst of rain.

24.2.3.head: حَفَشَ
24.2.3.meaning: Swept along or lashed, here the force of rain against the hillocks.

24.2.4.head: أَكَمَة
24.2.4.meaning: A low hill or mound, caught in the squall.

24.2.5.head: وابِل
24.2.5.meaning: A heavy downpour with large drops.

25.2.6.head: حامِل
25.2.6.meaning: Carrying the rider. Tha'lab also allows the boy as subject, driving the horse as he wills.

26.2.2.head: تَوالٍ
26.2.2.meaning: The trailing parts, here the hind legs and quarters of the galloping horse.

26.2.3.head: صِياب
26.2.3.meaning: True to their course. The forelegs are going exactly where the horse aims.

27.1.3.head: عَير
27.1.3.meaning: A male ass, here the wild jack picked out from his herd.

27.1.6.head: إِلف
27.1.6.meaning: Familiar company, here the females from which the jack has been separated.

27.2.4.head: نَسا
27.2.4.meaning: A vein or sinew running down the thigh and leg, here marked by blood.

27.2.5.head: فائِل
27.2.5.meaning: A vessel at the socket of the hip, a vulnerable place on the quarry.

28.1.3.head: نَضا
28.1.3.meaning: Drew out ahead of the other horses on the way home.

28.2.2.head: رُسغ
28.2.2.meaning: The pastern, the jointed lower part of the leg above the hoof.

28.2.3.head: عامِلَة
28.2.3.meaning: A weight-bearing limb that does the work of carrying the horse in a gallop.

29.1.2.head: مَيعَة
29.1.2.meaning: A surge of energy or impetus in a horse’s run.

29.1.4-5.head: مَوضِع الرُّمح
29.1.4-5.meaning: “The place of the lance”, the withers across which a horseman could lay his lance.

30.1.1.head: أَبيَض
30.1.1.meaning: Of unstained honour, an old epithet of praise.

30.2.2.head: مُعتَفٍ
30.2.2.meaning: A petitioner who comes to someone of means for help.

30.2.4.head: أَغَبَّ
30.2.4.meaning: Came on alternate days. His gifts never miss their day.

31.2.3.head: الصَّريم
31.2.3.meaning: Sirim can mean late night or dawn. A different gloss makes it a stretch of sand.

31.2.4.head: عاذِلَة
31.2.4.meaning: A woman who reproves. The women of Hisn’s household are concerned about his giving.

32.1.1.head: فَدّى
32.1.1.meaning: Addressed him with “May I be your ransom”, a formula of endearment.

32.2.5.head: مَختَل
32.2.5.meaning: An opening through which someone might be got round.

33.1.5.head: مُرَزَّأ
33.1.5.meaning: One whose resources are repeatedly drawn on by those who ask.

33.2.1.head: عَزوم
33.2.1.meaning: Resolute, firm in carrying an intention through.

34.2.5.head: نائِل
34.2.5.meaning: What others receive from him. His gifts can use up a fortune.

35.1.5.head: تَهَلَّلَ
35.1.5.meaning: Lit up with pleasure, as a face brightens to welcome a visitor.

36.1.3.meaning: Remote, here the distance between two branches of a family.

36.1.5.head: وَصَلَ
36.1.5.meaning: Kept up a tie of kinship, here by giving financial help.

37.1.2.head: نِعمَة
37.1.2.meaning: A favour. The verse couples seeing a kindness through with acknowledging one.

38.2.5.head: مَفصِل
38.2.5.meaning: A joint, used of the exact point at which an argument can be resolved.

39.2.3.head: أَلَمَّ
39.2.3.meaning: Came briefly to mind. The two m sounds are separated in the conditional form. The man says whatever occurs to him.

40.1.1.head: عَبَأَ
40.1.1.meaning: Mustered or made ready. The resource being gathered here is self-command.

40.2.5.head: مَقتَل
40.2.5.meaning: A vital spot, here any exposed weakness through which an opponent might be hurt.

41.1.1.head: حُذَيفَة
41.1.1.meaning: Hudhayfa ibn Badr of Fazara, the father of the man Zuhayr praises.

41.1.3.head: بَدر
41.1.3.meaning: Badr is Hisn’s grandfather and Hudhayfa’s father.

41.2.2.head: باذِخ
41.2.2.meaning: Lofty or towering, here a height of inherited standing.

42.1.3.head: حِصن
42.1.3.meaning: Hisn ibn Hudhayfa ibn Badr of Fazara, the subject of this praise poem.

42.2.2.head: ضَيم
42.2.2.meaning: An injury or humiliation imposed by force.

43.1.3.head: النُّعمان
43.1.3.meaning: Al-Nu'man, a Lakhmid king of al-Hira. Tha'lab tells of his quarrel with Hisn.

43.1.4-5.head: حَرَقَ نابَه
43.1.4-5.meaning: “Ground his fang”, clenched and ground his teeth in anger.

43.2.2.head: أَفضى
43.2.2.meaning: Went out onto open ground, without a city wall to shelter him.

43.2.4.head: مَعقِل
43.2.4.meaning: A stronghold or place of refuge. His swords fulfil the work of fortifications.

44.1.4.head: الحَليفان
44.1.4.meaning: The two allies are Banu Asad and Ghatafan in Tha'lab’s explanation.

44.2.2.head: لَجَب
44.2.2.meaning: The mingled din of many voices in a host.

44.2.3.head: لَجَّة
44.2.3.meaning: The clamour of voices raised together. Tha'lab’s main text has “its voices”, while the apparatus records the recited wording.

44.2.4.head: صاهِلَة
44.2.4.meaning: A neighing horse. The plural sets the sound of the horses beside the men’s voices.

45.1.5-6.head: رَملَة عالِج
45.1.5-6.meaning: The sands of Alij, a dune country named as the distant limit of the army’s effect.

45.2.3.head: الغَور
45.2.3.meaning: Low country. Abu Ubayda’s gloss includes the lowlands of Tihama.

45.2.5.head: زَلزَلَة
45.2.5.meaning: An upheaval. Al-Asma'i understands the lowlander’s calamities to be dispelled by Hisn.

46.1.2.head: خِباء
46.1.2.meaning: A tent, and by extension the household living under it.

46.1.4-5.head: ذات البَين
46.1.4-5.meaning: “What lies between them”, the state of relations within the household.

46.2.6.head: آجِل
46.2.6.meaning: The person who brought something about. Abu Ubayd explains that the speaker himself caused the quarrel.

47.1.3.head: ساعٍ
47.1.3.meaning: Someone hurrying to the scene. The culprit joins the people coming for news.
